text: Rain arrives at seven tonight.
I have eight hours to build a shelter from what this forest gives me.
My only guide: my grandmother's journal, from 1968.
She camped by a waterfall out here. Let's find it.
Grandma's directions: 'Left at the split boulder.' Fifty-eight years, and it's still split.
No trail signs in her day, just landmarks. I carry a map and compass too.
That's her, 1968. She's eighty-four now. She gave me this journal with one rule: read each page only on its night. And one request...
Tell me if the waterfall still sings.
I promised to bring her the sound.
Same rock. Same falls.
Grandma's exact spot. But see those logs jammed up here? Floodwater put them there. Not tonight.
Uphill, away from flood channels, two hundred feet from water. Local rules first.
This is an established campsite, with an old stone fire ring on bare soil. Campfires are allowed here today.
No dead limbs overhead. Level ground. And I have permission to camp here.
Two trees, each with a fork at chest height.
A dead, fallen ridge pole. Sound and straight.
It rests in both forks. A simple tie only stops it rolling.
Two hard tugs. Nothing shifts.
A quick check, not a guarantee. No cracks, no movement.
I copied Grandma's shallow angle first.
Then rebuilt it steeper, feet braced against logs to help stop sliding.
Her drawing is neater. Mine should shed rain faster. I hope.
Grandma used ferns. I'm using fir boughs from last week's storm.
Bottom first, each layer overlapping. Boughs leave gaps, so this is an experiment, not a waterproof roof.
Light along the ridge. That's a likely leak point.
One more overlapping layer on top. Better. Not perfect.
Dry leaves for the floor. Pad and bag stay sealed until I trust this roof.
An insulated sleeping pad cuts heat loss to the ground. Dry leaves add a little more.
How long will it hold? That's tonight's experiment.
Water before any fire. A pot to drink, a bucket for the fire.
Cloth removes debris. Boiling disinfects: one full minute at a rolling boil. We're low, so one minute.
Grandma's note: 'Drank from the falls. Stomach regretted it.' Even in 1968, a bad idea.
Five meters to the nearest bough, and upwind. If the wind rises, the fire goes out.
Dry, fallen wood. No rain in days, so there's plenty.
That should do.
Grandma's note: 'Fire on the first strike.' Then, smaller: 'Ha.' I brought a lighter.
One click.
There.
Feed it slowly.
Afternoon: watched an otter in the pool for an hour. Built nothing. Regretted it at nine.
Dinner. Grandma's journal says: 'Soup. Again.' Mine is noodles.
And dried sausage, sliced at home.
Hot handle. Something between me and the metal.
One pot, no dishes. Worth it.
Rain at seven. Fire goes out before I leave it. Drown it.
Stir the coals, the edges. Drown it again.
Then check, without touching. Nothing warm.
Half past six. Early. Of course.
No thunder forecast. I keep checking, and I'd leave well before any storm.
Hear thunder? Go to the visitor center, fifteen minutes away. No shelter out here protects you from lightning.
Eight o'clock. And... a leak by my feet.
Grandma's old mug. Forty summers of trips, and tonight it catches my leak.
My roof managed ninety minutes. Not perfect, but I'm staying dry.
Tonight's entry. Her rule, so I couldn't read it until now.
June fourteenth, 1968. Fern roof finished at six. Rain at nine. Roof held until ten.
Slept in a wet sweater. Happiest I have ever been. I write down every mistake, so the next one is new.
Sorry, Grandma. I changed straight into dry sleeping clothes. Wet clothes chill you fast.
Dear Grandma,
I found your waterfall. There was flood debris at your spot, so I camped uphill. Yours held an hour. Mine leaked at eight.
So, like you, I'm writing it down.
And yes. The waterfall still sings. Listen.
Morning. Wet, but rested.
Fire ring checked again: cold.
Ropes, padding, every scrap packed out. The boughs go back to the brush pile.
Page two: the pine with your initials. Love, Elise.
